newsitem.title: FRANCE: Nothing goes right for France's Juppe.
newsitem.headline: Nothing goes right for France's Juppe.

text.p: With the return of bombers and strikers, the bungling of another privatisation and mounting dissent on his centre-right coalition backbenches, nothing seems to be going right for French Prime Minister Alain Juppe.

The government was forced to make a humiliating U-turn and postpone the sale of electronics and defence giant Thomson SA on Wednesday after an independent privatisation commission refused to approve the takeover of its multimedia subsidiary by Daewoo of South Korea.
"This is one more shambles," fumed Francois-Michel Gonnot, centre-right chairman of parliament's influential industry and trade committee.

The left-wing opposition hailed the decision as a victory for Thomson's workers, who feared for their jobs and working conditions, and a slap in the face for Juppe, who announced his preference for the bid put together by Lagardere Groupe and Daewoo without waiting for the commission's opinion.
"The government was under so much pressure. It doesn't come as a surprise," one Paris stock market broker said. "It probably puts Juppe under more pressure."
It was the second time in a month the government had been forced to suspend a privatisation after the collapse of its bid to sell off Credit Industriel et Commercial (CIC) bank.
Juppe has also shelved a plan to restructure the SNCF state railway and create a separate railtrack company in the face of opposition by militant rail unions.

To avert a major labour revolt on the scale of last year's 24-day transport strike, he conceded retirement at 55 and new worktime regulations last week to end a 12-day blockade of French roads by striking truckers.
No sooner was that dispute settled than suspected Moslem fundamentalist bombers added to his woes.

A gas-canister bomb tore apart a Paris subway train on Tuesday, killing two people and signaling the return of indiscriminate bombings to the French capital more than a year after the government thought it had ended the previous wave.

A gloomy Juppe told parliament that France had once again become a target. Opposition leaders rallied behind the cabinet as it moved quickly to put more police and soldiers on patrol in city centres, at big stores, on public transport and at borders.
But the display of national unity against the bombers did nothing to strengthen Juppe's position, despite repeated statements of support by President Jacques Chirac.
Shares in retail stores and hotels fell sharply on the Paris bourse because of fears that the bomb would drive away tourists and deter Christmas shoppers.

In parliament, Juppe suffered the indignity of watching his own Gaullist RPR backbenchers give an ovation last week to ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing for a speech which savaged the government's monetary policy.
Now he is being forced to beat a retreat in the face of revolts by centre-right deputies over a plan to cap wealth tax for the very rich and a proposed tougher anti-racism law.
Parliamentary sources said Juppe had made clear to Gaullist RPR and centre-right UDF deputies that he would not insist on either piece of legislation if they opposed them.

Copies of this week's Newsweek magazine, which splashes the question "If Chirac and Juppe are so clever, how come France is in a mess?" on its front page, were circulating like subversive literature on the coalition's backbenches.

Some political analysts said the accumulation of cave-ins, mistakes and bad luck meant the president might be forced to reconsider changing prime minister, and not just reshuffling his cabinet, in a New Year shake-up.
But there is no sign so far that Chirac's confidence in Juppe is waning.
